summary: This memo specifies a subset of the distribution protocol used by BITNET LISTSERV to deliver messages to large numbers of recipients. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A mailing list sends one message to many people. This paper explains the way one big list program handed out those messages efficiently to lots of readers.

questions: how does bitnet listserv distribute mail
how to use the distribute protocol for mailing lists
subtitle: A protocol for bulk email delivery to large mailing lists

tldr.problem: Running large mailing lists with traditional mail server software (sendmail) causes severe delays; delivering to thousands of recipients is slow and resource-intensive.
tldr.mechanism: The DISTRIBUTE protocol, developed on BITNET, optimizes bulk delivery by routing a single message through a network of specialized servers, using topological information to send one copy per network link to multiple recipients, then expanding locally.
tldr.outcome: Mailing lists of 1,000+ subscribers can achieve 5- to 15-minute turnaround instead of hours, and the protocol is simple enough for non-BITNET sites to use via a standard SMTP interface.

today: RFC 1429 is informational and describes a practical protocol developed on BITNET. DISTRIBUTE is not widely used outside BITNET/LISTSERV environments, and modern mailing-list software uses other mechanisms. However, the RFC remains interesting as documentation of how BITNET solved the large-list delivery problem before modern mail infrastructure.

sections.title: The DISTRIBUTE Protocol
sections.content:
BITNET, in the mid-1980s, faced the problem of distributing messages to tens of thousands of subscribers efficiently. The LISTSERV software developed a specialized protocol called DISTRIBUTE to handle bulk mail delivery at scale. This RFC describes how non-BITNET users and other mailing-list applications can use the DISTRIBUTE service by submitting requests to a BITNET LISTSERV server via SMTP.

The key insight is that DISTRIBUTE uses topological information about the network to minimize redundant message copies. Rather than sending one copy per recipient (which wastes bandwidth), the server sends one copy toward a region, and that region's server forwards to its sub-regions, reducing traffic on heavily loaded links.

By the time this RFC was written, the DISTRIBUTE protocol was carrying 2 to 6 million messages per day on BITNET.
sections.plainLanguage: LISTSERV is a tool for running big mailing lists. Instead of sending a message to every person separately, it sends one copy down smart routes so the network is used efficiently.

sections.title: How to Find and Use a DISTRIBUTE Server
sections.content:
To use DISTRIBUTE, the first step is choosing a server in your topological vicinity—ideally geographically and network-wise close to your recipient base.

For testing only, you can use LISTSERV@SEARN.SUNET.SE (a Swedish server). For production, you should:

  • Verify the server has good connectivity (avoid sites using slow 9.6k leased lines for BITNET if they have fast IP access elsewhere).
  • Check the server version is 1.7f or higher (earlier versions have problems with long lines).
  • Ensure the server's Master nodes file is current (not older than 2 months).
  • Contact the administrator if you plan more than 10,000 daily recipients, to respect any usage policies or scheduled downtime.

A site directory of suitable production servers is planned for future publication. The DISTRIBUTE server itself is accessed via SMTP: you mail your distribution request to an address like LISTSERV@server.host.
sections.plainLanguage: Pick a LISTSERV computer near you, check it's up to date, and then send a special email to it with your list of recipients.

sections.title: Format of a DISTRIBUTE Request
sections.content:
A DISTRIBUTE request is a special email to the LISTSERV server. The body contains a structured format with four parts:

  1. JOB card: Marks the start and optionally names the job. Syntax: //jobname JOB ECHO=NO. The ECHO=NO keyword is required for production (suppresses resource-usage summaries). Omit it for testing.
  2. DISTRIBUTE command: DISTRIBUTE MAIL for production, or with options like ACK=MAIL (request acknowledgement), DEBUG=YES (show routing without delivering), or TRACE=YES (show routing and deliver).
  3. Recipient list: Wrapped in //To DD * and /* markers. Each recipient is on one line as user@host.com BSMTP. Addresses must be fully qualified; the keyword BSMTP means 'do not rewrite the header.' Restrictions apply: no quoted addresses except at the start of the local part, no leading asterisks (without quoting), no blanks in addresses.
  4. Message text: Wrapped in //Data DD *,EOF. The EOF keyword means the message extends to the end; otherwise add /* and // EOJ markers to delimit the message.

The MAIL FROM header should point to the list administrator or a human who can handle bounces. The From: field in the message body should match the MAIL FROM address (or an 'owner-' variant) to prevent mail loops.
sections.plainLanguage: The special email has sections for setup, which recipients to send to, and then the actual message. Each section has markers so the server knows where one part ends and the next begins.

sections.title: Routing and Performance
sections.content:
DISTRIBUTE servers maintain a nodes file describing the network topology—which other servers can reach which regions. When a message arrives, the server uses this information to decide where to forward the message.

For recipients in the local domain, the message is passed directly to the local SMTP agent. For remote recipients, the server routes the message through intermediate DISTRIBUTE servers to reach that region. A single message may be copied at intermediate points, but the key is that one copy is sent per remote server, not per remote recipient.

The DEBUG=YES option shows the routing plan without actually delivering, allowing you to verify efficiency before running for real. The output shows, for instance: 'Recipients at ABC.COM go to SEARN' and 'Recipients at UBVM go to UGA,' with a count of how many recipients are routed to each server.

Typical turnaround times are 5 to 15 minutes for BITNET recipients and 5 to 20 minutes for Internet recipients that can be routed through the server's topology tables. Unroutable recipients (for which no topological information exists) may take longer but usually faster than vanilla sendmail.
sections.plainLanguage: The server looks up where each recipient's computer is on the network map and forwards the message along the shortest path, batching multiple recipients per path.

sections.title: Example: Using the Protocol
sections.content:
To distribute a message to 5 recipients with the DEBUG option (to preview routing):

//Test JOB
Distribute mail Ack=mail Debug=yes
//To DD *
joe@ws-4.xyz.edu BSMTP
jack@abc.com BSMTP
jim@tamvm1.bitnet BSMTP
jill@alpha.cc.buffalo.edu BSMTP
james@library.rice.edu BSMTP
/*
//Data DD *,EOF
Date:         Tue, 19 Jan 1993 10:57:29 -0500
From:         Robert H. Smith <RHS@eta.abc.com>
Subject:      Re: Problem with V5.41
To:           somelist@some.host.edu

I agree with Jack, V5.41 is not a stable release...

The LISTSERV server responds with debug output showing the routing decisions:

ABC.COM goes to SEARN (213) - single recipient
UBVM goes to UGA (027) - single recipient
RICEVM1 goes to UGA - single recipient

For actual delivery, change the JOB card to //Test JOB Echo=NO and remove or change the DEBUG option. For silent production delivery, use Distribute mail without ACK=mail.
sections.plainLanguage: You paste in the names of the recipients and your message, the server shows you how it will route them, and then you can run it for real.
